reconcile.connective: Gill argues "doing good" in John 5:29 is not natural virtue but grace-enabled obedience worked in believers -- leaving Paul's verdict on the unconverted untouched.

discrepancy.connective: Robert G. Ingersoll pressed the sharper point: if total depravity brands even a mother's love and a stranger's charity sin, no coherent "good" is left for John or Paul to reward.

skeptic.name: Robert G. Ingersoll
skeptic.attribution: Robert G. Ingersoll (1833-1899), Heretics and Heresies (lecture, 1874)

excerpts.excerpt_text: they that have done good; which none of Adam's posterity naturally do, or can do of themselves: such are designed here who believe in Christ, which to do is the work of God, and the greatest and best of worlds; and without which it is impossible to please God in any; and indeed, whatever is not of faith is sin, and cannot be a good work: a good work is that which is done according to the will of God, from love to him, in faith, and with a view to his glory …
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Gill's comment on the very verse that requires 'doing good' (John 5:29) concedes no one naturally does good -- agreeing with the total-depravity texts -- and relocates 'good' to grace-enabled faith-obedience, which is the harmonizing move the row needs.

pd_work.resource: John Gill, Exposition of the Entire Bible (1746-63), comment on John 5:29
pd_work.author: John Gill
pd_work.note: Gill treats this exact tension directly in his comment on John 5:29, distinguishing the natural human inability the total-depravity texts describe from the grace-enabled 'good work' of believers, which he grounds in faith rather than unaided human virtue.
